text.front:
Bradwardine's Antiquity: History, Authority, and Pseudepigraphy
in the Sermo epinicius
Bernhard Hollick
University of Oslo / University of Cologne
KEYWORDS Bradwardine; Sermo epinicius (Victory Sermon), classicism; hermetism; pseudepigraphy; mythography
text.body:
When clergymen in fourteenth-century England entered the pulpit, it was not only Holy Scripture
they had in mind. Many sermons in that period were full of references and allusions to ancient
poetry, mythology, and history. 1 The occupation with the fabulae poetarum became a trademark
of preachers such as the Benedictine bishops John Sheppey (d. 1360) and Thomas Brinton (d.
1389), as well as a stumbling block for more austere minds such as the theologians John
Baconthorpe (d. 1346) and John Wyclif (d. 1384). 2 Classicism was not limited to one specific literary
genre, though. Sermons were just the epicenter of a growing body of texts which dealt in one way or
another with the ancient literary heritage, among them theological and exegetical works such as
Robert Holcot's (d. 1349) Super sapientiam Salomonis, homiletic handbooks, and example collec-
tions such as John Bromyard's (d. c. 1352) Summa praedicantium, or commentaries on pagan
and patristic authors, several of which were published by the chronicler, theologian, and literary
scholar Nicholas Trevet (d. c. 1328) (e.g. on Virgil, Seneca, and Augustine). 3
Thomas Bradwardine (d. 1349) was a typical representative of the learned, clerical milieu in
which Anglo-Latin classicism flourished. 4 He studied and taught in Oxford, before joining the
household of Richard de Bury (d. 1345), the bibliophile bishop of Durham (where he probably
met his fellow classicist Holcot). 5 Unfortunately, his career as a churchman and a writer was cut
short, when he succumbed to the plague, only one month after his appointment as archbishop

3 Trevet's ground-breaking exposition of De civitate Dei inspired similar works by English scholars such as Thomas Waleys, John

Medium Aevum, 25 (1956), 140-53.

4 Since Beryl Smalley published English Friars and Antiquity in the Early Fourteenth Century (Oxford: Blackwell, 1960), classicism in
late medieval England is often connected with the mendicant orders. However, neither were all classicists friars, nor did this
literary movement come to an end after the death of the last of the friars discussed in her study, John Lathbury in 1362. Secular
clerics such as Bradwardine or Benedictine writers such as the above mentioned Sheppey and Brinton, as well as Thomas Wal-
singham and John Wheathampstead contributed to the classical tradition; Wheathampstead also showed an early interest in

background. They all belonged to the university-trained clerical elites, usually in some way connected with Oxford.
text.body:
of Canterbury. Bradwardine's occupation with antiquity becomes evident in his major theological
work, De causa Dei contra Pelagium. His reading habits had a significant impact on his preaching -
at least as far as we can tell from his only surviving sermon. The Sermo epinicius was delivered at the
request of Edward III in Calais (1312-77), on the occasion of the victorious battle of Crécy in 1346. 6
Bradwardine addressed his mainly aristocratic audience in Middle English. 7 At the request of the
papal legate Cardinal Annibaldo di Ceccano (c. 1282-1350), bishop of Frascati, he later composed
an expanded Latin version. 8 Only the later revision survives in one incomplete copy (Oxford, Mer-
ton College, MS 180, fols 183 r -188 v ). 9 The Sermo epinicius bears witness to Bradwardine's erudi-
tion. Throughout his theological explanations, he invokes ancient authorities -or so he thinks,
since the actual classics are joint by pseudepigraphic and hermetic sources. Yet the scholarly surface
of the sermon is not just decoration. For Bradwardine, such references are a tool to negotiate his
attitude to antiquity. How and why he does so, is the topic of the following investigation.
Bradwardine's Theology and the Sermo epinicius
The battle of Crécy was not England's only military success in 1346. The armies of Edward III pre-
vailed in several battles against the French, the Irish, and the Scots. 10 In the Sermo epinicius, Brad-
wardine discusses the possible reasons for these victories, and in doing so, draws heavily on the
theology of De causa Dei contra Pelagium, which centres on a radical concept of divine causality. 11
According to Bradwardine, God is not only the origin of all creatures, he also participates in their
perdurance and agency:
Sciunt enim philosophi, et theologi non ignorant, quod quaelibet creatura facta a Deo semper essendo depen-
det ab eo, tanquam a suo necessario conservante; quare et similiter faciendo, nec per se sufficit aliquid agere
sine Deo, idem specialiter coagente, imo et principaliter praeagente. 12
[For the philosophers know and the theologians are not unaware, that any creature made by God always
depends on him for its being, just as from its necessary preserver; in a similar way, when it comes to its activity,
it cannot act by itself without God, who likewise specifically coacts and indeed even principally preacts].
This remarkable passage outlines Bradwardine's concept of divine causality and hints at the histori-
cal narrative which runs through De causa Dei contra Pelagium. As the title suggests, Bradwardine
pleads the case of God against the fourth-century theologian Pelagius who clashed with Augustine
about the role of divine grace and human free will for salvation, and his successors in the past and
present. In Bradwardine's eyes, the term 'Pelagianism' does not merely describe only one specific
text.note:

Frankfurt am Main: Minerva, 1964), p. 131.
MEDIEVAL SERMON STUDIES
text.body:
late antique heresy. Instead, it refers to an error which is the root of false believe in general: the fail-
ure to recognize God as the first cause and, as a consequence, the denial of the radical dependence of
everything created on his grace. As the archetypical heresy, Pelagianism was not invented by its
eponymous theologian. Both orthodoxy and heresy have supernatural roots which date back to
the beginnings of creation. The father of Pelagianism is Lucifer, who wanted to be equal, not sub-
ordinate, to God, thereby practically refusing to accept him as the first cause, while his adversary,
Michael, came to the defence of that hierarchy. 13 Consequently, Bradwardine was not just meditat-
ing on one theological problem among others, but on what he considered to be the quintessential
conflict at the heart of intellectual history from Adam and his offspring to the fourteenth century,
when Pelagianism was, according to De causa Dei contra Pelagium, very much alive in the lecture
halls of Oxford and other universities. 14
But despite the dichotomy at its centre, Bradwardine's historical narrative is in other regards dis-
tinctively syncretistic. As the stated concordance between theologians and philosophers indicates,
orthodox views can also be found in the works of non-Christian thinkers. Bradwardine includes
even the poets in his great consensus. 15 In some cases he goes as far as to treat them as philosophers:
Ovid, for example, is counted among the Platonists. 16 This assessment has practical consequences,
as Bradwardine supplies his thoughts with excessive lists of authorities. His witnesses against Pela-
gius are the Bible, the Church Fathers, and other scholastics, together with pagan, Jewish, and Isla-
mic philosophers, Sibylline and hermetic sources, as well as classical poets such as Virgil and Ovid.
He is significantly less meticulous when introducing the culprits, even though he presents their
views in much detail in the first corollary of De causa Dei contra Pelagium. 17 Sometimes, he refers
to them only with generic terms such as idolaters, Pelagians, or philosophers. 18 In principle, he
avoids naming contemporaries, no matter if he agrees with them or not. 19
In the Sermo epinicius, Bradwardine does not explicitly speak about Pelagius or Pelagianism. It is
easy, though, to discover a similar line of thought to that which he sets out in De causa Dei contra
Pelagium. 20 The main part of the sermon is dedicated to the refutation of certain common miscon-
ceptions. Some people believe that victory in battle is the consequence of celestial constellations,
favourable timing, fortune, fate, prudence, or pagan deities of love. 21 But as Bradwardine explains,
none of these assumptions are valid. God alone grants victory. 22 Believing anything else is intellec-
tually and morally wrong: 'Unde claret perspicue illos non parum peccare et divinam iracundiam
provocare, qui gracias sive grates victorie debitas creatori auferentes ab eo tribuunt creature'
text.note:
13 Bradwardine, De causa Dei, ed. by Savile, p. b v : 'Primo namque horum [Pelagianorum] haeresiarcha Lucifero, nolente Deo sub-
esse sed coesse, per Michaelem deiecto, surrexit Caim existimans peccatorem nequaquam iustificari gratis a Deo per gratiam
gratis datam, sed per meritum antecedens'.
14 Bradwardine, De causa Dei, ed. by Savile, p. 308, where he confesses his own Pelagian past.

15 See, for example, Bradwardine, De causa Dei, ed. by Savile, p. 135: 'omnes quoque gentes, Hebraei, Graeci, Latini et barbari,
omnes prophetae, omnes theologi et poetae et omnes philosophi ante Aristotelem') and p. 136 ('omnes patres tui, omnes
philosophi, prophetae, theologi et poetae'.

16 Bradwardine, De causa Dei, ed. by Savile, pp. 108 ('Plato, Ovidius, et Platonici caeteri') and 112 ('Ovidius Platonicus'). Similar
remarks appear in other works by contemporary English scholastics. See Robert Holcot, 'Utrum Theologia sit scientia: A Quo-
dlibet Question of Robert Holcot, OP', ed. by Joseph T. Muckle, in Mediaeval Studies, 20 (1958), 127-53 (p. 146), who mentions a
'responsio ad Platonem, Trismegistum, Apuleium, Avicennam et Ovidium et omnes alios'.
17 Bradwardine, De causa Dei, ed. by Savile, pp. 3-145.

18 An instructive example can be found in Bradwardine, De causa Dei, ed. by Savile, p. 23, where he scolds the 'Pelagian[i] seu
Cainit[ae] fingentes Deum nulli beneficium gratis dare, sed tantum pro suo merito praedecente'. While he conceals the specific
addressees of this criticism, he supports his objections with several classical authorities: Hesiod, Homer, Chrysippus, Seneca,
and Aristotle, as well as the 'veteres Graecorum poetae'. He is not always as oblique: on p. 119, he attributes the (in his eyes)
false assumption that the world is eternal explicitly to Aristotle (who appears on both sides of the theological divide explored
in De causa Dei contra Pelagium, even though much more often as a witness for Bradwardine's own views).

19 See Leff, Bradwardine and the Pelagians, p. 115. This is a contrast to the tendency of his time to refer to others (including
opponents) by name; see William J. Courtenay, Changing Approaches to Fourteenth-Century Thought (Toronto: Pontifical Insti-
tute of Mediaeval Studies, 2007), pp. 24-27.
20 Dolnikowski, 'Thomas Bradwardine's Sermo Epinicius', p. 360.
21 Bradwardine, Sermo epicinius, ed. by Offler, § 3, p. 17.

22 Bradwardine, Sermo epicinius, ed. by Offler, § 5, p. 17-19: 'Quicquid Deus vult fore seu fieri, illud fiet, quemcunque Deus vult
vincere, ille vincet, et quemcunque Deus vult regnare, ille regnabit'.
B. HOLLICK
text.body:
['Therefore it is evident that they commit no small sin and provoke God's rage, who detract the
gratitude and thanks owed to the creator for victory from him and instead bestow them to the crea-
ture']. 23 This is nothing less than a practical application of the idea of divine co-efficiency: England's
recent success on the battlefield is explained by an act of grace, not by any created cause. Human
agency is not irrelevant, but it is instrumental, insofar as it only implements God's will. 24
Less attention has been paid to historical thought in the Sermo epinicius than to theology of grace
and political propaganda. This reluctance is understandable since history is not an obvious topic in
the sermon. One must follow the clues Bradwardine provides for his readers to discover the very
same ideas that are developed systematically in De causa Dei contra Pelagium. An important tool
in this hidden messaging is the use of authorities.
The Use of Authorities in the Sermo epinicius
Bradwardine's discussion of the reasons for military success is embedded in a dense web of quota-
tions, references, and allusions. As in De causa Dei contra Pelagium, the 'doctor profundus' does not
treat all sides equally: the adherents of the six false reasons for victory remain vague. Bradwardine
neither names them nor quotes from their writings. In most cases he refers to general group iden-
tities, for example to the Egyptians, ancient Jews, or unspecified astrologers. If he feels the need to
use names, he chooses biblical figures who represent the respective heresies, such as Nimrod, Reho-
boam, and Sennacherib, who stand for those who overestimate their own powers. 25 Bradwardine is
aware that some of the views that he renounces in his sermon are very much alive even within his
own church. About the 'vani astrologi' of his time who believe that victory depends on celestial con-
stellations, he notes:
Set hii sunt similes antiquis gentilibus, qui solem et lunam et stellas ceteras tanquam deos ex causis huiusmodi
coluerunt. Tales si quidem sint huius temporis Christiani, videbuntur antichristiani pocius nuncupandi seu
Christiani apostate […]. Hii igitur horribiliter deviant et aberrant. 26
[But they are similar to the ancient pagans, who worshipped the sun and the moon and the other stars as gods
for such reasons. If the Christians of this time are indeed so, they should apparently be called rather anti-
Christians or Christian apostates […]. In this, they are horribly wrong and misled].
As before, no names are mentioned. By erasing the individuality of his opponents even more rig-
orously than in De causa Dei contra Pelagium, Bradwardine creates a collective identity. They
belong to one faceless group of heretics, united by the same underlying mistake: the failure to
understand the absolute dependence of all creation on God. 27
A different picture emerges in the case of authorities who support Bradwardine's views. Here, the
veil of anonymity is suddenly lifted. Often, their names are revealed together with quotations from
their writings. Not surprisingly, Holy Scripture is omnipresent. The Church Fathers also make their
expected appearance. Secular and canon law, on the other hand, are only mentioned once. 28
Corresponding to the classicizing taste of his time and milieu, Bradwardine mentions the ancient
text.note: 23 Bradwardine, Sermo epicinius, ed. by Offler, § 5, p. 18.

24 Bradwardine, Sermo epicinius, ed. by Offler, § 26, p. 27: 'Set hic fortassis aliquis presumens de viribus propriis cogitabit: "Quid
igitur facit humana potencia et hominis fortitudo?" Cui breviter respondendum: Certe hoc facit, quod Deus per illum facere
disponebat. Deus enim est quasi vir pugnator, homo autem sicud glaudius aut baculus seu quodlibet instrumentum huiusmodi
in manu ipsius'. Bradwardine's insistence on God's causality seems sometimes very deterministic. In De causa Dei contra Pela-
gium, he tries to reconcile divine omnipotence with human freedom. Whether his solution leaves any room for the latter has
been subject to debate, newer studies tend to agree that it does (see Theo Kobusch, Die Philosophie des Hoch-und Spätmit-
telalters (Munich: Beck, 2011), pp. 444-48), while earlier scholars have drawn a more deterministic picture of Bradwardine's
thought (for example Leff, Bradwardine and the Pelagians, p. 87, even though he does not forget to mention Bradwardine's
'assertion of human free will and freedom as existing through God's determinism').
25 See Bradwardine, Sermo epicinius, ed. by Offler § 19, p. 24.
26 Bradwardine, Sermo epicinius, ed. by Offler, § 4, p. 17.
27 In Bradwardine, Sermo epicinius, ed. by Offler § 4, p. 17, he even mentions a Jewish sect which worshipped the moon as Diana.
28 See Bradwardine, Sermo epicinius, ed. by Offler, § 5, p. 18: 'iura canonica atque civilia'.
MEDIEVAL SERMON STUDIES
text.body:
thinkers Aristotle (to whom he refers either by his name or the common epithet 'philosophus'),
Plato, and Boethius. Flavius Josephus is present with citations from both the Bellum Iudaicum
and the Antiquitates Iudaicae. Such authentic works are supplemented with the pseudo-Ovidian
De vetula and several texts erroneously attributed to Aristotle: De mundo, De bona fortuna
(which is composed of material from the Eudemian Ethics and Magna moralia, which attribution
to Aristostle is doubtful), and the Secretum secretorum (referred to as Epistola [Aristotelis] ad Alex-
andrum). The latter is not the only hermetic source in the Sermo epinicius: the Asclepius (under the
widespread title De verbo aeterno) and another treatise, De mundo et caelo, found their way in the
sermon. 29 Both texts are attributed to Hermes Trismegistus. Despite originating from different his-
torical and religious settings, in Bradwardine's view all these authorities agree in principle with one
another. As in De causa Dei contra Pelagium, he stresses the concordance between philosophers and
theologians -no fewer than three times in the short text. 30 Casually, he remarks that the same is
true for the 'historiae veteres et recentes', i.e. historiography from different times. 31 However, before
the philosophers can come to an understanding with theology, they must agree among themselves.
And indeed, in his discussion of fortune Bradwardine claims that the position of Aristotle, the Phi-
losopher, is held by philosophers in general. 32 Of course, his intention is not to deny that there are
contradictions in his vast variety of source material, but to show that these are not the inherent con-
sequence of philosophical research. While Bradwardine decries astrological ideas from ancient
Egypt, his counterargument is purely rational: it points at a fallacy in his opponents' views. The
error of the 'sapientes Egipcii' results from a wrong conclusion drawn from the observation of
the world and can be corrected within a philosophical framework. 33
The boldest expression of Bradwardine's syncretism appears in a passage dedicated to the pun-
ishment of sinners in the afterlife, where he links Aristotle's and Christ's words on bodily mortality:
Cum igitur secundum Philosophum mors consueta momentanee transcurrenda ultimum terribilium iudice-
tur, quam terribilis mors predicta! Quare et Veritas ipsa monet: Ne terreamini ab eis, qui occidunt corpus et
post hec non habent amplius quid faciant: timite eum, qui postquam occideret, habet potestatem mittere in
gehennam. Ita dico vobis, hunc timite. 34
[Since according to the Philosopher the ordinary death which one must go through quickly is judged to be the
last of all horrors, how terrible is the predicted death! Therefore, also the Truth itself admonishes: Do not be
afraid of those who kill the body and afterwards do not have anything more they can do; fear him, who after he
has killed, has the power to send you to hell. So, I tell you, fear this one].
Bradwardine seemingly treats Aristotle and Christ as authorities of equal dignity. The adverb quare
even constructs a logical connection between their words. This harmonizing impression is common
in his writings, although it is partly misleading; Bradwardine indeed tends to collect as many
authorities as possible in order to illustrate general support for his own ideas. But the alleged agree-
ment is based on a hierarchical order of sources, even if this is not always obvious. Bradwardine calls
Christ the 'summus philosophus'. 35 Hereby, he underlines that any philosophical investigation, if
properly conducted, will eventually lead to the same truth, the doctrines of the Christian faith, as
far as they are comprehensible without direct access to Holy Scripture. Faith is the aim and perfec-
tion of philosophy, as Bradwardine states in De causa Dei contra Pelagium: 'vera philosophia in

31 Bradwardine, Sermo epicinius, ed. by Offler, § 36, p. 37.
32 Bradwardine, Sermo epicinius, ed. by Offler, § 11, p. 20 ('secundum Philosophum, ymmo secundum philosophos').
33 Bradwardine, Sermo epicinius, ed. by Offler, § 7, pp. 18-19.

34 Bradwardine, Sermo epicinius, ed. by Offler, § 34, p. 34; Bradwardine referrers to Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics III.6 1115a26 and
quotes Luke 12. 4-5.
35 Bradwardine, Sermo epicinius, ed. by Offler, § 28, p. 28.
B. HOLLICK
text.body:
cognoscenda divinitate et sancta divinaque religione consistit' ['true philosophy consists in recog-
nizing the deity and the holy and divine religion']. 36 In the Sermo epinicius as well as in De causa Dei
contra Pelagium, authorities do not represent a plurality of opinions, but are treated as expressions
of two antagonistic and archetypical world views centred around the problem of divine causality.
Poetry and Myth in the Sermo Epinicius
Attentive readers of the Sermo epinicius may notice that unlike in De causa Dei contra Pelagium, Brad-
wardine does not include the poets in his consensus of philosophers, theologians, lawyers, and histor-
iographers. His silence on their role is even more surprising considering that the sermon contains
several verses from classical and classicizing sources, as well as allusions to Greco-Roman mythology
(which was, according to Bradwardine and many other medieval scholars, a poetic invention). 37 In
order to solve this apparent conundrum, a closer look at the respective passages is necessary.
Two of the authorities in verse -both simply referred to as 'poeta' -deal with philosophical,
not mythological or otherwise fictional matters. 38 Ovid serves as witness for the assumption that an
omen is granted by God as an act of grace (which vice versa points back to its author). 39 The quota-
tion, however, is partly Bradwardine's own making, who joined two originally separate hexameters
from the Epistulae ex Ponto:
Omnia sunt hominum tenui pendencia filo.
Ludit in humanis divina potencia rebus. 40
[Everything human is hanging on a fragile threat.
Divine power plays with human affairs].
Obviously, theses verses do not require much hermeneutic effort. They allow Bradwardine to treat
Ovid as a source for natural theology. The other couplet, echoing Claudian, offers political thoughts,
which were equally unproblematic from a contemporary perspective. 41 A larger challenge is posed
by mythological stories or images. Due to their pagan content, they were hard to accept for Chris-
tians when understood literally. Luckily, ancient and medieval mythography offered a variety of sol-
utions, several of which Bradwardine applies in his sermon. The simplest method is perhaps the
most modern: refusing to take the words of the poets seriously. When Bradwardine speaks of
the strategic superiority of England's enemies, he compares both sides with partly historical, partly
mythical figures from Roman literature:
Aut que proporcio prudencie Anglicorum ad prudenciam Gallicorum? Certe, sicud Pisonis et Mercurii sive
Apollinis. Ipsi nanque sunt Argus, Anglici Polliphemus. Habent enim mille consiliarios contra unum de
nostris. 42
[Or in which proportion stands the prudence of the English to the prudence of the French? Surely as that of
Piso, and [on the other side] that of Mercury or Apollo. For they are Argus, and the English are Polyphemus,
since they have a thousand advisors against one of ours].
text.note:

MEDIEVAL SERMON STUDIES
text.body:
Bradwardine does not seek for any hidden truth here. Cyclops or giants with a hundred eyes simply
help him to illustrate his point. Elsewhere, he draws more profound insights from pagan myth. For
that purpose, he relies sometimes on allegorical interpretations, whose central idea is summarized
in the Philobiblon, a treatise on collecting books usually attributed to his patron Richard de Bury:
'Ubi ficta sed honesta tractatur sententia, naturalis vel historialis veritas indagatur sub eloquio typi-
cae fictionis' ['Where a fictious but becoming subject is treated, natural or historical truth is exam-
ined under the rhetorical guise of allegorical fiction']. 43 Some medieval scholars -among them the
anonymous author of the French Ovide moralisé and Pierre Bersuire in his Latin Ovidius moraliza-
tus, went even further and offered Christian expositions of the Metamorphoses. This was attractive
for preachers, since it enabled them to convey a moral or religious message wrapped into an enter-
taining story. However, Bradwardine's use of allegory is much more cautious. In the Sermo epini-
cius, he writes about the Roman goddess Fortuna:
Illa nanque dea fortune ceca apud hos veteres dicebatur et inter picturas eorum depingebatur ut mulier que-
dam ceca, eo quod sine discrescione aut meritis personarum distribuit prospera vel adversa. 44
[For this goddess of fortune was said by those elders to be blind and was painted in their pictures as a blind
woman, because she distributes good and bad luck without discretion and regardless of the merits of persons].
Bradwardine points out a figurative meaning, which was, in his eyes, intended by the pagans who
invented the mythic goddess, instead of searching for a distinctively Christian meaning. It is worth
noting that his interpretation does focus on the attributes of the deity, not on the plot of any myth
surrounding her. His exposition of Fortuna's blindness is a (very simple) application of the 'pic-
tura'-technique which became fashionable in the early fourteenth century (skilful examples can
be found in Ridevall and Holcot). 45 The most striking fact, though, is how Bradwardine proceeds:
Set quam ceca insania colere talem deam, que cultores suos videre non potest nec inter cultores et contemp-
tores discernere! Neque enim magis prodesset colere quam contempnere talem deam. Adhuc autem, hec secta
nedum est irracionalis et insana, verum eciam heretica et prophana. 46
[But what a blind madness it is to worship such a goddess, who can neither see her worshippers nor dis-
tinguish between worshippers and those who despise her. For it is not of more use to worship than to disdain
such a goddess. But besides, this sect is not only irrational and insane, but also heretical and profane].
Suddenly, Bradwardine's attention shifts from the figurative meaning of Fortuna's attributes to the
historical reality of her veneration. A similar interest in ancient religion reappears elsewhere in the
Sermo epinicius. While discussing different concepts of fate, Bradwardine quotes the only verse with
non-philosophical content in the whole sermon, a popular line by an unknown poet about the three
Fates: 'Cloto colum baiulat, Lachesis trahit, Atropos occat' ['Clotho holds the distaff, Lachesis draws
out [the threat] and Atropos cuts [it]']. 47 As he explains, this myth is a poetic depiction of a pagan
belief:
Aliqui nanque putant per fatum dictum a fando, quod famen vere deorum gentilium seu dearum circa tem-
poralia specialiter autem humana coerciat et disponat. Unde poete fingunt tres sorores fatales facta hominum
disponentes. 48
[For some people believe, because the word 'fate' comes from 'fari' [to utter], that the speech of the pagan gods
and goddesses truly controls and administers temporal, but especially human affairs. Therefore, the poets
invented three fateful sisters who administer the deeds of men].

B. HOLLICK
text.body:
Bradwardine adds one more similar observation at the end of his sermon, where he repudiates the
idea that sexual prowess leads to military success. 49 There he talks about adherents of pagan deities
connected with lust and sexuality: Hymen/Cupid, Venus and Aphrodite. He also includes Epicurus
in his list. 50 It is unclear, though, whether this happened by mistake or if he intentionally mixed-up
cults and philosophies. The decisive point is that he treats all of these figures similarly to how pre-
viously he has discussed the Fates -not just as allegories, but as deities who were really worshipped
in antiquity. Their cult was more than the product of an imagination run wild. Bradwardine blames
the poets for their role in the formation of paganism, but he does not accuse them of making the
pantheon up entirely. They merely deceive their audience about the nature of their supposed gods:
Omnes nanque deos gentilium sive deas demones esse constat, sicud dicebatur. Unde et vere dicit Philoso-
phus: 'Multa menciuntur poete'. Quis autem Christianus pro triumpho de hostibus demonibus referat gracias
et non Deo? 51
[For it is certain that all gods and goddesses of the pagans are demons, as said before. And therefore, the Phi-
losopher rightly says: 'The poets tell a lot of lies'. But what kind of Christian gives thanks to the demons and
not God for the triumph over his enemies?]
The pagan gods grew from actual religious practises in which supernatural beings were involved,
although the worshippers were mistaken about their identity. 52 This was not a new idea. Bradwar-
dine himself alludes to Psalm 95. 5: 'quoniam omnes dii gentium daemonia' ['for all the gods of the
heathens are demons'], hereby tying in with an exegetical tradition, which reaches back to the
Church Fathers. 53 He is not blindly following authorities, though. Instead, Bradwardine is imple-
menting his own philosophical project. His aim was not to assimilate pagan authors, but to
point out their place in the continuous struggle between orthodoxy and Pelagianism. Classical
mythology was, in his eyes, primarily a source for past beliefs. The claim, that the gods were demons
provided him with the proper fundament for his historicizing hermeneutics (which fits neatly to the
assumption that Lucifer himself is the forefather of Pelagianism). Here, too, Bradwardine is follow-
ing a general trend in the fourteenth century. A similar interest in the formation of ancient religion
can be observed, for example, in Ridevall's Fulgentius metaforalis, according to which paganism
roots in memorial culture. 54
Bradwardine's approach to poetry in the Sermo epinicius is different to that in De causa Dei contra
Pelagium. In his theological magnum opus, he neither adheres to one distinct hermeneutic method
nor focuses on a specific topic; instead, his interpretations depend very much on the needs of the par-
ticular context. In the Sermo epinicius he deals with such material in a much more homogenous and
systematic way. He uses philosophical verse as confirmation of his own thoughts and mythological
narratives as historical documentation. Herein probably lies the reason why Bradwardine omits the
poets in the Sermo epinicius when he speaks of a concordance of theologians and philosophers.
Like many other medieval scholars, he understood poetry not primarily as a text in verse, but as a
text.note: 49 Bradwardine, Sermo epicinius, ed. by Offler, § § 32-36, pp. 32-37.
50 Bradwardine, Sermo epicinius, ed. by Offler, § 32, p. 32.

51 Bradwardine, Sermo epicinius, ed. by Offler, § 14, pp. 21-22. The demonic nature of pagan idols is stressed again in § 32, p. 32:
'Quid enim est iste deus huius amoris nisi, sicud ceteri dii gencium, demonium: demon luxurie, incentor luxurie et nutritor?'

52 Bradwardine understands that the ancient 'daímones' are not identical with Christian demons; but, as he explains in Bradwar-
dine, Sermo epicinius, ed. by Offler, § 14, p. 22, even if we consider them like Plato as 'dii secundi', they are subject to God, who
therefore alone deserves gratitude for victory.

53 E.g. in Augustine, De civitate Dei 9,23, ed. by Bernhard Dombart and Alphons Kalb, Corpus Christianorum Series Latina, 47
(Turnhout: Brepols, 1955), p. 269: '"Super omnes" ergo "deos" dixit, sed "gentium", id est quos gentes pro diis habent,
quae sunt "daemonia"'.

54 John Ridevall, Fulgentius metaforalis, ed. by Hans Liebeschütz (Leipzig: Teubner, 1926), pp. 65-71, where he elaborates on
Fulgentius, Mitologiae, in: Fabii Planciadis Fulgentii V.C. Opera, ed. by Rudolf Helm (Leipzig: Teubner, 1898), pp. 3-80 (1,1,
pp. 15-17). Towards the end of the century, this historical turn could get even more radical: Thomas Walsingham's Archana
deorum, written around 1400, treats Ovid's Metamorphoses as a pagan text (the parallels to Boccaccio are evident, even though
there are no signs that he knew the Genealogia deorum).
MEDIEVAL SERMON STUDIES
text.body:
fabula (fiction). 55 Hence, he considered the quotations from Ovid and Claudian as philosophical
statements. That which is strictly speaking poetic, on the other hand, the stories about pagan deities,
is rarely appropriated by allegorical readings, but accepted as a more or less accurate account of
ancient religion -and as such, cannot be part of the orthodox consensus.
Hermetism and History
Bradwardine's use of authorities rests on the assumption that there is a general consensus between them
(or, more precisely, two antagonistic consensus, one orthodox, one heretical). But where does the
internal cohesion in each of these two groups come from? In the case of the heretics, Bradwardine
does not state any direct link between them, neither in the Sermo epinicius nor in De causa Dei contra
Pelagium. However, they are, as he wrote in his comparison of astrologists and ancient pagans quoted
above, 'similes'. They result from the very same mistake, namely the failure to recognize God as the first
cause -a failure whose original and archetypical instance was the Fall of the Devil.
The prevalence of the orthodox view on divine causality beyond the Judaeo-Christian tradition
was much more difficult to explain. Bradwardine had to show that pagan writers were able to gather
a certain amount of reliable religious insights without ever having read or even heard of Holy Scrip-
ture. Earlier theologians often believed that it was by reason alone that non-Christians uncovered if
not the whole truth, at least parts of it -the 'praeambula fidei', as Aquinas said, such as the exist-
ence of God or the creation of the world. 56 But in the early fourteenth century, this epistemological
optimism became increasingly contested. William of Ockham was significantly less enthusiastic
about the possibility of a rational approach to God than Aquinas. 57 His moderate scepticism forced
him to recalibrate the relationship of theology and philosophy. This affected immediately the atti-
tude to the classical heritage and other non-Christian authorities. If faith is the only way to know
God, pagan authors without access to divine revelation have not much to say in religious matters. 58
Bradwardine's ostentatious classicism indicates his disagreement with the 'venerabilis incep-
tor'. 59 At the same time, he was aware that a return to earlier epistemologies was not a viable option.
He had to answer Ockham's criticism of reason. His solution was to turn to the history of knowl-
edge. While the confined space of the Sermo epinicius did not allow him to develop his respective
ideas in much detail, he gives some clues. The references to hermetic literature and to the Antiqui-
tates Iudaicae suggest a historical connection between divine revelation and philosophy. In order to
ensure that none of his readers misses that point, Bradwardine adds a short sketch of such a gen-
ealogy of knowledge, while discussing different concepts of fate. Only one is acceptable for Chris-
tians: 'fatum' can be understood as deriving 'a fando seu famine summi Dei' ['from the uttering or
the speech of the highest God']. 60 Bradwardine introduces a number of authorities in favour of this
text.note:

gratia, vult aliquod verum factum mystice nuntiare. Haec enim fabulae species videtur congruere rhetoricis et poetis. Multi

B. HOLLICK
text.body:
concept, starting with Hermes Trismegistus, followed by Plato and Aristotle and finally by Augus-
tine and Boethius. 61 In the end, he adds some quotations from the Bible. Bradwardine places these
authorities, except for the Bible, in an (assumed) chronological order; moreover, he hints at a
relationship between them which goes much further than the similarity between heresies when
he calls Hermes the 'pater philosophorum', Plato and Aristotle his sons. 62 The language of kinship
indicates that later philosophers indeed build their systems on the teachings of this legendary sage.
Boethius and Augustine, on the other hand, were Christians. They could rely on Holy Scripture, not
just on the philosophical tradition. But nonetheless, it is 'nec mirum' that they agree with Hermes
and his offspring, since similar ideas can be found in the Genesis and in the psalms. 63 In the Sermo
epinicius, Bradwardine does not fully disclose the underlying historical narrative. Yet in De causa
Dei contra Pelagium, this issue is explored in much detail: Hermes Trismegistus is the first authority
quoted in the opening chapter, where the 'pater philosophorum' is also introduced as 'rex Aegypti,
philosophus et propheta'. 64 Each of these epithets indicates a possible source of cognition. In the
case of 'philosophus' (reason) and 'propheta' (revelation), this is obvious. For Bradwardine's histor-
icization of epistemology, the reference to Egypt is of no less importance, since it explains, how bib-
lical wisdom spread in the ancient world. Hermes was foremost a mediator for the teachings of the
patriarchs and prophets of the Old Testament. Since Bradwardine relies on several sources, his
account is not entirely coherent. Sometimes, Hermes is replaced by other figures such as Seth
and Solomon. The basic idea, however, is always the same. Primordial wisdom, revealed to the
Israelites, found its way to other places and peoples, who built their philosophies thereupon:
Philosophus quoque in Secreto secretorum partis secundi primo, Deus, inquit, excelsus et gloriosus ordinavit
modum et remedium ad temperantiam humorum et ad conservantiam sanitatis et ad plurima alia acquirenda;
et revelavit ea sanctis prophetis servis suis et iustis prophetis suis et quibusdam aliis, quos praeelegit, et illus-
travit spiritu divinae sapientiae et dotavit eos dotibus scientiae. Ab istis sequentes viri philosophiae principa-
tum et originem habuerunt, Indi et Perses et Graeci et Latini ab istis hauserunt et scripserunt artium et
scientiarum principia et secreta, quia in scripturis ipsorum nihil falsum, nihil reprobum invenitur, sed a
sapientibus approbatum. 65
[The Philosopher also says in the first chapter of the second part of 'The Secret of Secrets': 'The heavenly and
glorious God has ordained a means and cure for tempering the humours and for the preservation of health
and for the acquisition of many other things. And he revealed them to his servants, the holy prophets, and to
his just prophets and to some others whom he preelected, and he illuminated them with the spirit of divine
wisdom and provided them with the gifts of knowledge. The men who followed received the principle and
origin of philosophy from them. The Indians, Persians, Greeks and Latins drew upon them and wrote
about the principles and secrets of the arts and sciences, since in their writings nothing false and nothing
base is found but only that which is approved by wise men].
The philosophers of later epochs had no fundamentally new or different insights by virtue of their
own reason; they were merely drawing conclusions from premises revealed by God:
Horum igitur patrum divinitus illuminatorum doctrinis doctissimis posteriores philosophi informati has glor-
iosas scientias conscripserunt et quaedam quodammodo alia non penitus aliena, quia ex primis illis fontibus
derivata, superaddiderunt. 66
[Hence the later philosophers, instructed in the most erudite teachings of those divinely illuminated fathers,
wrote these glorious sciences down and they further added something in a certain manner different, [but] not
entirely foreign, since it was derived from those first sources].

text.body:
In other words, wherever pagan philosophers were right, they merely spelled out divine revelation.
In this sense, they anticipated the work of scholastic theology. Therefore, Bradwardine's historical
narrative has dramatic epistemological consequences: the question of how far reason can reach
without God's guidance becomes obsolete, since it is always preceded by faith.
Pseudepigrapha and the Appropriation of Ancient Authorities
The hermetic frame narrative was not all Bradwardine's pseudepigraphic sources had to offer. In
addition, they worked in favour of his attempt to integrate as much of the classical heritage as poss-
ible into his own theology, since they contaminated authors such as Aristotle and Ovid with ideas
which narrowed the distance to Christian beliefs. Thereby, pseudepigrapha supported the assump-
tion that the classics belong to the same tradition as the prophets, patriarchs and Church Fathers. In
the following, this transformative force will be exemplified by some remarks on the use of De
mundo and De vetula in the Sermo epinicius.
De mundo: Beyond the Unmoved Mover
Bradwardine refers twice to the pseudo-Aristotelian De mundo, a small treatise influenced by several
ancient philosophical schools (Aristotelianism, Platonism, stoicism, Neopythagoreanism; Christianity
had no perceivable impact). 67 The author and dating of De mundo are still subject to discussion. 68 In
the Middle Ages, it was mostly considered to be an Aristotelian work, although not without excep-
tions. The Jewish philosopher Moses Maimonides, much valued by many scholastics including Brad-
wardine, firmly denied its authenticity. 69 In Bradwardine's days, De mundo was widely read, since it
met theological needs. The unmoved mover in Aristotle's Metaphysics takes no part in the sublunar
realm. The god of De mundo, on the other hand, although still transcendent, is involved in the world,
not unlike Plato's demiurge. 70 He is creating, preserving, and ordering everything with his powers (i.e.
while he is no part of the world, he is able to affect it in all its aspects). He even works miracles. 71
Bradwardine realised the possibilities a more active image of God opened up for his own sermon.
He mentions De mundo for the first time while dealing with different concepts of fortuna:
Unde et Philosophus in libris suis De mundo et De bona fortuna discusciens de fortuna reducit illam princi-
paliter in Deum et operacionem divinam, cui et consonans Augustinus eandem sentenciam plene docet. 72
[Therefore, also the Philosopher in his books 'On the world' and 'On good fortune', when he investigates for-
tune, reduces it in the first place to God and divine work; Augustine, agreeing with him, teaches exactly the
same opinion].
Bradwardine probably has a passage from De mundo in mind, according to which fortuna is just one
of many names for Jupiter. 73 In De bona fortuna respectively the Eudemian Ethics, Aristotle himself

text.body:
explains that impulses which drive a lucky person to make the right decision are caused by God. 74
One might object that in this context causation does not mean divine providence, but simply the
activity of a first mover, which affects the soul as much as anything else in the world. But combined,
the references to De mundo and De bona fortuna seem to suggest that Aristotle understood 'fortuna'
in a similar way to Augustine, who reminded his readers in Contra academicos that 'etenim fortasse
quae vulgo fortuna nominatur, occulto quodam ordine regitur' ['indeed, maybe, what commonly is
called fortune, is governed by some hidden order']. 75
Further on in the Sermo epinicius, in his historical sketch of the proper understanding of fate as
famen Dei, Bradwardine even paraphrases a paragraph from De mundo, where Pseudo-Aristotle
presents yet another interpretation of the three Fates. In this, they are exposed as representatives
of the past, present, and future -'et omnia prorsus fatalia reducunt in Deum hec omnia tempor-
ibus omnibus moderantem' ['and they reduce everything fateful entirely to God, who guides all of
this in all times']. 76 The interpretation of the Fates as such is not particularly surprising, since it
was promoted, among others, by Augustine in Contra Faustum. 77 The source is decisive: Brad-
wardine was able to quote a text allegedly written by the most prominent pagan philosopher in
order to confirm that already from an ancient Greek perspective, fate was nothing other than
divine providence. It is easy to see why Bradwardine was so attracted to De mundo. If this little
treatise were to be accepted as an Aristotelian work, the Stagirite suddenly seems to propose a
theology very different from that of the Physics and Metaphysics. The introverted, unmoved
mover yields to a god who is deeply engaged in worldly, including human, affairs. This blunt
act of revisionism allows Bradwardine to include Aristotle into the ancestral gallery of his own
teachings about a creator who is preserving and controlling the world and all of its inhabitants
at every moment of their existence.
De vetula: The Conversion of Ovid
With the quotation from the pseudo-Ovidian De vetula, Bradwardine communicates a similar
message. This fictional autobiography began to spread fast after 1250. 78 It was widely read in

bekana, recensio Vulgata, ed. by Valérie Cordonier, 2016, Aristoteles Latinus Database [http://www.brepolis.com, 8, 14 (1248a);
accessed 12 March 2023]: 'Quod autem queritur hoc est, quid motus principium in anima. Palam quemadmodum in toto deus,
et omne illud: movet enim aliquo modo omnia quod in nobis divinum. Rationis autem principium non ratio, sed aliquid melius.
Quid igitur utique erit melius et scientia et intellectu nisi deus? Virtus enim intellectus organum. Et propter hoc, quod olim
dicebatur, bene fortunati vocantur qui si impetum faciant, dirigunt sine ratione existentes, et consiliari non expedit ipsis:
habent enim principium tale quod melius intellectu et consilio, qui autem rationem, hoc autem non habent, neque divinos
instinctus, hoc non possunt'.

75 Augustinus, Contra academicos, ed. by W.M. Green, Corpus Christianorum Series Latina, 29 (Turnhout: Brepols, 1970), 1,1,1,
pp. 3-61 (p. 3); in Retractiones, ed. by Almut Mutzenbecher, Corpus Christianorum Series Latina, 57 (Turnhout: Brepols,
1984), 1,1,2, p. 7, he is even stricter: he warns against the 'pessima consuetud[o], ubi dici debet: hoc deus voluit, dicere:
hoc voluit fortuna'.

76 Bradwardine, Sermo epicinius, ed. by Offler, § 16, p. 22, who is referring here to De mundo, ed. by Lorimer and Minio-Paluello,
p. 49 (7, 401b): 'Nam tria Fata secundum tempora distincta, filum vero fusi hoc quidem factum, illud vero futurum, aliud vero
torquetur. Est autem statutum in facto quidem unum Fatorum, Atropos dictum eo quod omnia que sunt facta immutabilia
sunt; in futuro vero Lachesis (…); in presenti vero Clotho, perficiens et torquens unicuique propria. Perficitur autem et fabula
non inordinate. Sunt autem hec omnia nichil aliud nisi Deus'.

77 Augustinus, Contra Faustum, ed. by Joseph Zycha, Corpus Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum Latinorum, 25 (Vienna: Verlag der Öster-
reichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften, 1891), 20, 9, pp. 251-797 (pp. 544-45): 'Habent quidem et illi quaedam fabulosa
figmenta, sed esse illas fabulas norunt et vel a poetis delectandi causa fictas esse adserunt vel eas ad naturam rerum vel mores
hominum interpretari conantur, sicut […] tria fata in colo et fuso digitisque filum ex lana torquentibus propter tria tempora,
praeteritum, quod in fuso iam netum atque involutum est, praesens, quod inter digitos nentis traicitur, futurum in lana, quae
colo inplicata est, quod adhuc per digitos nentis ad fusum tamquam per praesens ad praeteritum traiciendum est'.

78 See Ralph J. Hexter, 'Shades of Ovid: Pseudo-(and para-)Ovidiana in the Middle Ages', in Ovid in the Middle Ages, ed. by Clark,
Coulson, and McKinley, pp. 284-309 (pp. 304-08); and Dorothy M. Robathan, 'Introduction to the Pseudo-Ovidian De vetula',
Transactions and Proceedings of the American Philological Association, 88 (1957), 197-207.
MEDIEVAL SERMON STUDIES
text.body:
England's learned circles. Among its readers, we can find at least two of Bradwardine's acquain-
tances: Richard de Bury and Robert Holcot. 79 The frequency with which De vetula in mentioned
in fourteenth century 'accessus ad auctores' suggests an even larger audience. 80 Yet not everybody
was convinced of its authenticity. Doubts began to rise almost immediately after its release, due
both to its anachronistic content and the obvious linguistic and metric differences to the rest of
the Corpus Ovidianum (even if we take into consideration that the latter comprised several pseu-
depigraphic works). 81 But the reckless rewriting of Ovid's life and thought was, also, what made
De vetula so popular. Bradwardine's use of the poem in the Sermo epinicius is an enlightening
example of its impact. It appears in a list of authorities against an astronomical concept of fate
together with Augustine, Gregory the Great and other unnamed 'patres catholici'. 82 Bradwardine
quotes: 'Est fatum fatuum: fatui qui fata secuntur' ['Fate is fatuous; fatuous are those who follow
the Fates']. 83 Other than mythological matters, these verses were applicable in a sermon without
any further hermeneutic efforts. They gave Bradwardine the opportunity to spread ideas under
Ovid's name which were at least compatible with his own Christian theology. 'Ovid' could be
quoted in one breath with the writings of the Church Fathers. True, as the lines from the Epistulae
ex Ponto have shown, the poet's original works were also able to provide such validation. But in
addition, the reference to De vetula invokes an Ovid who went through a profound change of
heart, which lead him from his juvenile hedonism to philosophical studies and in the end almost
to Christianity. 84 This biographical arc has an epistemological dimension, since it reflects a tra-
ditional medieval curriculum, in which secular knowledge leads to the threshold of the mysteries
of faith. Therefore, De vetula propagates exactly the inclusive ideal of learning which shaped the
Sermo epinicius as well as other works written by the 'doctor profundus'.
The question remains whether and to what extent Bradwardine was aware that some of his key
sources were of a pseudepigraphic nature, given the fact that doubts about several of them (not De
mundo and De vetula, but also the Secretum secretorum) had arisen already in the Middle Ages. 85 At
least in the last case they were shared by Bradwardine, who refers in De causa Dei contra Pelagium
to the author of De vetula with the strangely aloof wording 'Ovidius ille' (which did not prevent him
from citing the text several times). 86 In the Sermo epinicius, no trace of these reservations is left.
Instead, the quotation from De vetula is the only case in which the (alleged) poet is named.
Given the fact that Bradwardine composed the Sermo epinicius parallel to his work on De causa
Dei contra Pelagium, it is likely that he consciously decided to remain silent about the problem
of authenticity within the much narrower remit of a sermon. 87 An Ovid almost converted to Chris-
tianity fits perfectly to his attempt to turn the classics into unconscious witnesses of the Christian
faith.
text.note:
79 See Richard de Bury, Philobiblon, ed. by Thomas, ch. 9, p. 83; on Holcot see Ralph Hanna, 'Robert Holcot and De vetula: Beyond
Smalley's Assessment', in Literary Theory and Criticism in the Later Middle Ages: Interpretation, Invention, Imagination, ed. by
Ardis Butterfield, Ian Johnson, and Andrew Kraebel (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2023), pp. 78-93.

80 See Wilken Engelbrecht, 'Carmina Pieridun multo vigilata labore / exponi, nulla certius urbe reor: Orléans and the Reception of
Ovid in the aetas Ovidiana in School Commentaries', Mittellateinisches Jahrbuch, 41 (2006), 209-26 (p. 211).

81 See Hexter, 'Shades of Ovid', p. 308; and Paul Klopsch, Pseudo-Ovidius de vetula: Untersuchungen und Text (Leiden: Brill, 1967),
pp. 82-83.
82 Bradwardine, Sermo epicinius, ed. by Offler, § 15, p. 22.

83 Bradwardine, Sermo epicinius, ed. by Offler, § 15, p. 22. In its original context, the verse has a slightly different meaning, see De
vetula, ed. by Paul Klopsch, in: Klopsch, Pseudo-Ovidius de vetula, pp. 193-290, 1,489-90 (p. 212): ' … nichil ergo / est fatum
fatuum; fatui qui fata sequuntur'.

84 De vetula, ed. by Klopsch, 3,611-811, pp. 272-78, where 'Ovid' led by astrological considerations almost embraces Christianity.
Other medieval biographers were less reluctant: according to them, 'sanctus Naso' became bishop of Tomis. See Bernhard
Bischoff, 'Eine mittelalterliche Ovid-Legende', in Bernhard Bischoff, Mittelalterliche Studien 1 (Stuttgart: Hiersemann, 1966),
pp. 144-49; Joseph B. Trapp, 'Ovid's Tomb: The Growth of a Legend from Eusebius to Laurence Sterne, Chateaubriand and
George Richmond', Journal of the Warburg and Courtauld Institutes, 36 (1973), 35-76 (pp. 42-43).

85 Steven J. Williams, The Secret of Secrets: The Scholarly Career of a Pseudo-Aristotelian Text in the Latin Middle Ages (Ann Arbor:
University of Michigan Press, 2003), pp. 305-11.
86 Bradwardine, De causa Dei, ed. by Savile, pp. 75 and 265.

87 De causa Dei contra Pelagium was published in 1346, but some passages are probably based on notes from Bradwardine's
teaching activity in Oxford. See Leff, Bradwardine and the Pelagians, pp. 265-66.
B. HOLLICK
text.body:
Conclusion
The classicism of Bradwardine's Sermo epinicius surely met the taste of fourteenth-century listeners
and readers. One cannot say for certain how much the orally-delivered sermon differed from the
surviving Latin revision. But the incessant criticism of 'poetic fables' and similar embellishments
is proof enough that such features were not confined to the written versions. Homiletic practice,
not model sermons sparked the anger of purists such as Wyclif. It is therefore fair to assume
that Bradwardine addressed his flock in Calais not without making any of the references above
-although in a different language. However, Bradwardine's stylistic choices were not simply a con-
cession to contemporary preaching habits. Rather, the Sermo epinicius applies an elaborate com-
munication strategy which playfully engages different audiences. First and foremost,
Bradwardine addresses the king and the military leadership of England's troops in France. For
those men, mythic exempla or scattered verses could lighten up an otherwise complex political
and theological lecture. Like other preachers, Bradwardine knew how to entertain a crowd. At
the same time, Bradwardine spoke to the clergy, particularly with the written version, which was
after all prepared at the request of a bishop and papal legate. He could -and did -expect a milieu
of university-trained theologians in Oxford, London, or Avignon, who shared his interest in anti-
quity and understood the philosophical problems which came along. For them, Bradwardine's
mosaic of classical, pseudepigraphic, and hermetic authorities conveyed an additional message: a
new outlook on ancient philosophy and poetry, as well as on their relationship to Christian
faith. This was not exclusively of homiletic or academic relevance. The more rigorous separation
of secular and religious knowledge in some forms of late scholasticism put the status of the learned
clerical elites as safeguards of a hard-to-acquire expertise in question. The Sermo epinicius is an
attempt to bridge that epistemological gap as well as a public act of cultural self-assertion amid
upheavals, whose full force began to be felt only in the decades after Bradwardine's death.
